analysis.one_liner: Applies the same child labor rules to farm work as to other jobs and toughens penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 19 cosponsors but never got a committee vote, and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended the special exemptions that let children work in agriculture under rules far looser than those covering every other kind of work. It would have barred children under 12 from farm jobs, raised the minimum age for hazardous farm work from 16 to 18, and increased fines and prison terms for employers who violate child labor laws. It also would have required employers to report injuries to workers under 18, added 100 federal child labor inspectors, tightened pesticide-safety rules for children and pregnant women in fields, and funded school dropout-prevention programs for migrant farmworker youth.
analysis.who_benefits: Children of migrant and seasonal farmworkers, who are currently allowed to work in agriculture at ages far younger than in any other industry. The bill would have raised minimum ages, restricted hazardous work to those 18 and older, given injured child workers the right to sue employers, and required better tracking of where and how children are hurt on farms. Farmworker families would also gain access to dropout-prevention programs with tutoring, mentoring, and stipends.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Fair Labor Standards Act exemptions that let children of any age work in agriculture outside school hours, applying the same age restrictions to farm work as to other jobs, and limits the family-farm exemption to work for a close family member on that family member's own farm [S2] [S3].

Raises the minimum age for hazardous agricultural work from 16 to 18, increases civil penalties to between $500 and $15,000, adds up to 5 years' imprisonment for willful or repeat violations that kill or permanently disable a minor worker, and creates a private right of action allowing injured child workers or their families to sue employers [S2] [S3].

Requires employers to report any injury or illness to a worker under 18 within five days, directs the Labor Department to compile public data on child employment and violations, and funds at least 100 additional Wage and Hour Division inspectors to enforce child labor laws [S2] [S3].

Directs the EPA to write stricter pesticide worker-protection standards accounting for children and pregnant and nursing women in and near treated fields, with reviews every five years, and funds competitive grants for dropout-prevention programs for migrant youth ages 12 to 18 [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Farm operators, particularly larger commercial agricultural employers who rely on young and adolescent workers at wages and ages below standard labor rules. They would face higher labor costs, a narrower family exemption, mandatory injury reporting, larger fines, possible criminal prosecution for repeat violations, and lawsuits from injured young workers.

drawbacks.text: The bill narrows the family-farm exemption to work performed for a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, first cousin, or legal guardian on that relative's own farm, which could sweep in some traditional extended-family farm arrangements that pose no danger to children [S3].

The enforcement provisions require new appropriations — at least 100 additional inspectors and a 10 percent budget increase for prosecution — and the dropout-prevention program is funded at 'the greater of $50,000,000' or current levels, so the bill's protections depend on Congress actually funding them [S3].

A new private right of action with attorney's fees could increase litigation against farm employers, a cost honest supporters would have to weigh against the deterrent value for cases of serious injury or death [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — holding agricultural employers to the same child labor standards as everyone else — addresses a well-documented gap: federal law has long allowed children to do farm work at ages, and in hazardous conditions, that are illegal in any other industry. The costs fall on a specific industry that has operated under a century-old carve-out, and the bill preserves a genuine family-farm exemption. The main design weakness is that enforcement and dropout-prevention funding depend on appropriations, and the narrowed family exemption could burden some harmless traditional arrangements.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to three subcommittees, none of which ever acted on it, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucille Roybal-Allard introduced the bill on June 19, 2001, with 18 original cosponsors, all but one of them Democrats [S1] [S3].

It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and the Agriculture Committee, and in June and August 2001 was sent to three subcommittees; the record shows no markup, hearing, or vote in either full committee [S5].

The bill had 19 cosponsors — 17 of 208 House Democrats, 1 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's 1 Independent — and never advanced past committee before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm employers kept the existing exemptions that allow children to work in agriculture at younger ages and in more hazardous conditions than other industries permit, with no new reporting duties, penalties, or inspectors. Farmworker children gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm employers relying on child labor exemptions

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no roll-call exists; support was heavily Democratic (17 of the 19 cosponsors), with 1 House Republican and the House's sole Independent also cosponsoring [S4].

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (fruit and vegetable growers and other farm operators)
industries.note: The bill would have removed the child labor exemptions agriculture uniquely enjoys, raising the minimum ages for farm work, mandating injury reporting, increasing penalties up to 5 years' imprisonment for fatal violations, and adding 100 enforcement inspectors. Farm employers benefit from being able to hire children at ages illegal in every other industry, and those savings come at the cost of children working in hazardous conditions.

industries.industry: Pesticide manufacturers and commercial farm applicators
industries.note: The bill directed the EPA to write stricter worker-protection standards accounting for children and pregnant or nursing women in and near treated fields, with five-year reviews and state-by-state inspection reporting. Compliance costs would fall on growers and, indirectly, on chemical makers whose products face tighter use rules.

The bill reserved funding for a national farmworker organization to run a participant database, a toll-free information line, and technical assistance for dropout-prevention grantees, and made the program available regardless of work authorization status.
